extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of communications, mass communication, and cultural studies
extracted.subtask_description: Interpretive and theoretical analysis of mass media and communication that situates news and other media forms within broader cultural worlds, comparing objectivist and expressivist traditions and assessing implications for public life and knowledge. Emphasizes hermeneutic methods, historical-empirical linkage, and the political/epistemological stakes of media models.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examine multiple cultural worlds and their interpenetration
rubrics_metrics.description: “The analysis of mass communication will have to examine the several cultural worlds in which people simultaneously exist—the tension, often radical tension, between them, the patterns of mood and motivation distinctive to each, and the interpenetration among them.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Investigate how popular art, science, religion, ordinary speech, leisure, ritual, and information constitute distinct but coexisting cultural worlds; map moods (e.g., sadness, joy) and motives (e.g., erotic, aggressive) distinctive to each world and ask whether and how they extend beyond their domains. Avoid assuming a single cultural hierarchy that privileges scientific motives as the final court of veridicalness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apply interpretive cultural science to characteristic media products
rubrics_metrics.description: “The task now for students of communications... is to turn these advances in the science of culture toward the characteristic products of contemporary life: news stories, bureaucratic language, love songs, political rhetoric, daytime serials, scientific reports, television drama, talk shows, and the wider world of contemporary leisure, ritual, and information.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use methods from phenomenology, hermeneutics, and literary criticism to analyze concrete media forms and genres; treat each product as a site for cultural interpretation rather than merely as data for positivist measurement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adopt a hermeneutic, conversational approach among scholars
rubrics_metrics.description: “The task of hermeneutics... is to charm hermetically sealed-off thinkers out of their self-enclosed practices and to see the relations among scholars as strands of a conversation... where the hope of agreement is never lost so long as the conversation lasts.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize interpretive dialogue across theoretical traditions; avoid presuppositions of a single universal method. Emphasize civility, plural perspectives, and conversation as a means to sharpen theory rather than seeking final adjudication by abstract foundations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use media-specific theoretical concepts and methods
rubrics_metrics.description: “The concepts and methods, which, if inadequate, are at least unembarrassing, when applied to interpersonal communication prove hapless and even a little silly when applied to the mass media.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not simply transplant interpersonal communication models to mass media research; incorporate questions of political power, institutional change, scale, and the mediated nature of publics when designing concepts and methods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Elucidate theoretical structures to support historical-empirical work
rubrics_metrics.description: “I am attempting to elucidate a theoretical structure that will support and give generality to detailed historical-empirical investigation.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Develop middle-range theoretical frameworks that can guide and generalize from specific historical and empirical studies (e.g., the telegraph → mass press example). Expect to proceed via detours rather than via pristine axiomatic systems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Situate research within objectivism vs. expressivism
rubrics_metrics.description: The chapter draws a fundamental distinction between “objectivism” (Cartesian, science-as-paradigm) and “expressivism” (reality as remade by human activity) and locates communications scholarship along this axis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be explicit about whether one treats starting points as noncontingent (objectivist) or historically contingent and produced (expressivist). Consider the three objectivist assumptions (noncontingency of starting points; indubitability; identity) and the expressivist counterclaims when framing questions and interpreting findings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat reality as historically produced rather than objectively given
rubrics_metrics.description: “Reality has been made—has been progressively made—by human activity... The history of the species is simultaneously the history of the transformation of reality.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid seeking Archimedean, timeless starting points. Analyze how technologies, social relations, and symbolic practices reconfigure what counts as reality; accept historically varying human purposes as the primary basing point for inquiry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emphasize cultural production and the role of the associative mind
rubrics_metrics.description: “The mind—the associative, cooperative mind—its extension in culture and realization in technique, is the most important means of production. The most important product of the mind is a produced and sustained reality.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyze how cognitive and social practices produce cultural artifacts and social reality; attend to techniques and symbolic labor as modes of production analogous to economic production.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reframe media problems from morals/power to epistemology/knowledge
rubrics_metrics.description: “Lippmann changed this problematic... He argued that a free system of communication will not guarantee perfect information, and therefore there are no guarantees of truth... Lippmann redeﬁned the problem of the press from one of morals and politics to one of epistemology.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating media systems, assess their epistemic capacities (how they produce, represent, and circulate knowledge and stereotypes) in addition to questions of power and freedom. Consider whether debates should prioritize what publics know and how reliably they know it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess news as signal/statistics vs. stereotype/degenerate representation
rubrics_metrics.description: “News can only give, like the blip on a sonar scope, a signal that something is happening. More often it provides degenerate photographs or a pseudo-reality of stereotypes... Where there is a good machinery of record, the news system works with precision; where there is not, it disseminates stereotypes.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate the capacity of news to ‘picture’ reality by asking whether the subject matter admits precise machinery of record (e.g., sports scores, stock prices) or whether it is contested and narrative-driven. Diagnose when news functions as signalling that prompts inquiry versus when it implants stereotypes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate news as occasion for public discussion (Dewey’s conversational model)
rubrics_metrics.description: Dewey argues that public opinion “is formed only in discussion, when it is made active in community life... publication is partial and the public which results is partially informed and formed until the meanings it purveys pass from mouth to mouth.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize the conditions for face-to-face and local conversational life that enable publics to form; assess media by their capacity to foster inquiry, dialogue, and participatory exchange rather than by their (impossible) capacity to deliver perfect representations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analyze the crisis of community life produced by instrumental communication
rubrics_metrics.description: “Language—the fundamental medium of human life—is increasingly defined as an instrument for manipulating objects... The divorce of truth from discourse and action—the instrumentalization of communication—has... disrupted the very notion of truth.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Investigate how prevailing communication models and practices (propaganda, polemic, instrumentality) undermine shared public space, impair the truth-revealing function of language, and erode civic capacities like following arguments and taking others’ points of view.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat communication as action/interaction that constitutes the world
rubrics_metrics.description: “We must... discard the view of language as reference, correspondence, and representation and the parallel view that the function of language is primarily to express assertions about the world. Then we must substitute the view that language—communication—is a form of action—or, better, interaction—that not merely represents or describes but actually molds or constitutes the world.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frame studies to show how communicative practices enact and reconfigure social reality; design analyses that foreground performative, constitutive, and associative aspects of language rather than mere referential accuracy.
